Guide

MOF Topology Studio reads a CIF, finds the building units, reduces the framework to a net, and names that net with the RCSR three-letter symbol. This page explains each step, how to read the results, and what to do when a result looks wrong.

Quick start

  1. Open Load sample in the side panel and click Open CIF…, or drop a .cif file anywhere on the window. To try the tool first, pick a structure under Load reference (HKUST-1, MOF-5, UiO-66, ZIF-8, a 2D COF and others).
  2. The result strip at the top shows the net symbol, connectivity, point symbol and whether the net is interpenetrated.
  3. Switch between Standard and All-node under Simplification to see both descriptions.
  4. Use the tabs for figures, building units, invariants and the report. Exports live in the Export panel.

Everything runs in your browser. The CIF is never uploaded, and nothing is kept after you close or refresh the page.

How it works

In short: the CIF is expanded and bonded, and guests are removed. Metal clusters become SBUs and carbon-containing parts become linkers. The framework is then reduced to a net (standard and all-node), described by its invariants and vertex figures, named against the RCSR library, and placed in the Reticular Chemistry 3.2 parent → derived scheme. In detail:

  1. Reads the CIF. Cell, symmetry operators and atom sites are read. If no operators are listed, they are generated from the space-group symbol. For disordered sites only the first disorder group is kept, and overlapping atoms are removed (the lower occupancy goes).
  2. Finds bonds. Two atoms are bonded when their distance is below the sum of covalent radii plus the bond tolerance (default 0.40 Å).
  3. Removes guests. Any molecule or ion that is not connected periodically (solvent, counter-ions) is removed and listed under “Guests removed”.
  4. Finds SBUs. Metal atoms are grouped with the O, OH, F or water bridging them. Metals bridged by one carboxylate-type group closer than the Max M···M limit (default 4.0 Å) join the same SBU, so a Cu paddle-wheel becomes one unit.
  5. Finds linkers. Everything containing carbon becomes an organic linker. Rings up to the largest ring size (default 16, enough for a porphyrin) are treated as one unit. In COFs the periodic organic framework is split into knots and linkers.
  6. Builds the net. Standard: one node per SBU and one per linker with three or more connections. All-node: linkers are split at branch points (rings or atoms with three or more arms). In both, nodes with one connection are removed and nodes with two become edges.
  7. Calculates invariants (coordination sequences to 10 shells, point symbols, interpenetration). It then compares them with the RCSR library (— nets); point symbols separate nets whose sequences coincide.
  8. Classifies vertex figures. Each node’s neighbour directions are matched to the closest ideal shape (triangle, square, octahedron, hexagonal prism…).
  9. Places the result in Reticular Chemistry 3.2. The standard and all-node nets are checked against the parent → derived/related tables (Chem. Rev. 2020, 120, 8039). Derived nets that are missing from the library get a tentative name from connectivity, vertex figures and parent.

Watch out for heavy disorder, rod SBUs (MOF-74, MIL-53) and nets outside the library. Cross-check unusual results with Systre, ToposPro or CrystalNets.jl (see Troubleshooting and Limits).

Standard vs all-node

A MOF can be simplified in more than one valid way. The app always calculates both of these:

Standard

Each SBU is one node and each linker is one node. Linkers joining only two SBUs become edges. This is the description most MOF papers quote, e.g. HKUST-1 = tbo, NOTT-100 = nbo.

All-node

SBUs stay single nodes, but each linker is split at its branch points (a ring or atom with three or more arms). A tetracarboxylate such as bptc becomes two 3-c nodes, so NOTT-100 becomes fof.

For simple linkers the two agree. When they differ, report both. The standard net shows how the building blocks are arranged, and the all-node net shows the full connectivity of a branched linker.

Reading the results

Net symbol
The RCSR name (e.g. pcu, fcu). A green RCSR match means every node’s coordination sequence and proportion match one library net.
RCSR · ambiguous
Several library nets share the same invariants; the most common MOF net is shown first. Nets such as sod/sod-b are the same graph with different colourings.
tentative · RC 3.2
The net is not in the drawing library, so a name is suggested from the Reticular Chemistry 3.2 tables using connectivity, vertex shapes and the parent net. Treat it as a lead and confirm it with Systre or ToposPro.
not in library
No match. The invariants are still valid; export the .cgd and check it with Systre, ToposPro or CrystalNets.jl.
Connectivity
Coordination numbers of the node classes, e.g. (3,4)-c, and how many distinct node classes there are (n-nodal).
Point symbol
For each node, the smallest ring (circuit) through each pair of its edges, written as {63} and so on. The subscript after each bracket gives the ratio of node classes.
Periodicity
3D net, 2D layers (COFs and layered MOFs), or 1D chains. “n-fold interpenetrated” means n identical nets thread through each other.
Colouring interpenetrated nets
Set Colour atoms by and/or Colour nodes by to “Net / layer” (Display panel). Each interpenetrating copy of the framework, or each stacked layer of a 2D structure, gets its own colour, and Net colours lets you change them.

The tabs

Structure & net
The crystal with the net drawn over it. Atoms are coloured by building unit and nodes by class. Buttons a, b, c look down each axis; iso resets. See View controls below for the mouse and keyboard.
Building units
One card per distinct SBU, linker or COF knot. Blue markers are points of extension (e.g. carboxylate carbons) and ochre markers are all-node branch points.
Ideal net
The ideal RCSR embedding of the matched net, coloured to match your node classes. Type any symbol to draw another net. The side panel lists example MOFs and parent/derived relations.
Invariants
Both schemes side by side, a table of node classes (vertex figure, point symbol, shortest circuits, coordination sequence N1–N10, TD10), a coordination-sequence plot against the RCSR reference, and edge classes and components.
Parent & derived
Where the result sits in the Reticular Chemistry 3.2 scheme, candidate names for nets missing from the library, and the full searchable tables.
Net library
MOF nets with example MOFs and CSD refcodes. Click a net to draw it.
Report
A publication write-up generated from the current analysis: a Methods paragraph (settings, simplification schemes, how nets were identified), a Results paragraph (node roles, vertex figures, connectivity, point symbol, RCSR net, interpenetration, all-node and Reticular Chemistry 3.2 naming), Table 1 of topological descriptors, a suggested figure caption and numbered references. Set the compound name, choose sections, then copy it as formatted text (pastes into Word with superscripts and italics), copy plain text, or save as .html or .doc. Below it is the full plain-text analysis report. Check the wording and references before submission.

View controls

  • Left drag: rotate. Rotation is free about the camera’s own axes, has no limit, and stops the instant the mouse does. Rotation sensitivity (Display panel) can slow it down for lining up a precise view. It only ever slows rotation, never speeds it up past the default, and resets to full speed the next time the file is opened rather than being remembered.
  • Shift + left drag: roll (rotate in the screen plane), for straightening a figure without changing what you’re looking at.
  • Alt + left drag: lasso select. Draw a freeform outline, and every atom projected inside it (host and guest together, whichever are currently shown) is added to the selection.
  • Ctrl + Alt + left drag: lasso select whole fragments. Same outline, but each atom it touches brings its entire fragment into the selection, using the same rule as Ctrl-click on a single atom. A fragment is a building unit (SBU or linker) or a guest molecule.
  • Click an atom or bond to add it to or remove it from the selection. Ctrl-click an atom to toggle its whole fragment. Clicking empty space clears the selection.
  • Lasso selection works on screen position only, not true depth. An atom behind another one is selected too if its projected position falls inside the outline, even though it’s hidden from view by whatever is in front of it. Rotating to a clearer angle before lassoing avoids surprises in a dense structure. This is separate from atoms that aren’t displayed (individually hidden, a hydrogen with H display switched off, or excluded by “Show ASU only”); those are never selected, by lasso or any other method.
  • Ctrl + Shift + left drag: move the whole structure (and its net) anywhere in the display area, without rotating it. Middle drag does the same. Double-click recentres it.
  • Orthographic / Pseudo-orthographic / Depth scaling (Display panel, Camera): three mutually exclusive camera modes. Orthographic (the default) is a true parallel projection, so unit-cell edges viewed straight down an axis overlay exactly; use it for figures aligned along a, b or c. Pseudo-orthographic and Depth scaling both use the same mechanism: a genuine perspective camera at a narrow angle, parked correspondingly far away, so nearer atoms and nodes are drawn slightly larger and far/near cell edges no longer overlay exactly edge-on-edge. The only difference is the angle. Pseudo-orthographic fixes it at a small, usually imperceptible 2°, while Depth scaling exposes it as a slider (2° up to 25°) for a deliberately stronger, adjustable sense of depth. This helps when judging a large structure’s 3D shape at a glance, where a true orthographic view can read as flat. The slider stays disabled, at whatever it was last set to, unless Depth scaling is selected. Because this app draws atoms back to front rather than with near/far clipping planes, zooming in close never clips through an atom in any mode. The camera mode applies to every view and to PNG/SVG exports.
  • Axis arrows (a, b, c): drag the axis indicator with the left mouse button to move it anywhere in the display. Double-click it to put it back in the bottom-left corner. The unit-cell outline uses the same colours: the a, b and c edges leaving the origin corner are drawn red, green and blue. Its position is kept in PNG/SVG exports, and Axes in the Display panel hides it.
  • Right drag, vertical: zoom (up = in, down = out). The mouse wheel is disabled.
  • Arrow keys rotate in fixed 5° steps: left/right about the vertical axis, up/down about the horizontal axis. Page Up / Page Down roll in 5° steps. Holding Shift with any of these six turns makes the 5° nudge an exact 90° turn instead, which is handy for snapping to a face-on view along whichever axis that key rotates about. (Ctrl was tried first, but Ctrl+Page Up/Page Down are already claimed by the browser’s previous/next-tab shortcut, so Shift is used throughout.)
  • − and = / + zoom out and in one fixed step at a time, the same as stepping the Set scale number down or up (Display panel).
  • Delete (or Backspace) deletes the selected atoms, or cuts the selected bonds if no atoms are selected. Because the structure is periodic, every symmetry image of a deleted atom or bond goes, and the topology is re-analysed straight away. Restore deleted (Edit atoms panel) undoes all deletions.
  • Ctrl+C generates a centroid from the selected atoms. It is drawn as a magenta marker and listed with its fractional coordinates in the Edit atoms panel.
  • Escape clears the whole selection. Space selects everything if nothing is selected, or clears the selection if anything is. Shift+Space inverts the atom selection; Ctrl+Space inverts the bond selection.
  • Ctrl+Z hides the selected atoms (same as “Hide selected” in the Edit atoms panel); Ctrl+U unhides everything. Hiding only changes the view, never the analysis.
  • For a CIF-based structure: a toggles between showing only the asymmetric unit and showing everything currently packed; c toggles the unit cell; h toggles hydrogen display; l toggles atom labels.
  • Rotation and zoom keys work on the Structure and Ideal net views; selection and editing keys work on the Structure view. Keys only respond while focus isn’t in a text box, dropdown or button, so click the structure first if a key seems to do nothing.

Parent & derived nets (Reticular Chemistry 3.2)

Chen, Jiang, Li, O’Keeffe & Eddaoudi (Chem. Rev. 2020, 120, 8039) start from edge-transitive binodal parent nets, such as alb, shp and rht. Replacing one kind of parent vertex with a small group of linked vertices gives a trinodal net of minimal transitivity [3 2]:

  • Derived: the other parent vertex keeps its coordination (e.g. alb → ury).
  • Related: that coordination increases (e.g. shp → pek, where squares become cubes).

For a MOF with branched linkers the standard scheme usually gives the parent and the all-node scheme the derived net. The authors recommend quoting both, e.g. “alb-derived ury net”, and the app writes that name for you. The CF (coordination figure) strings such as [33]X2 come straight from the paper: [XmY]Zn means a Y vertex linked to m X and n Z vertices, and * marks a shape that has morphed from the parent.

Vertex-figure symbols

Each node’s neighbours define a coordination shape. The app matches it to the closest ideal polyhedron by comparing all neighbour–neighbour angles (hover the symbol for the RMS deviation). Switch on Vertex figures under Display to draw these shapes (the augmented-net view).

CNSymbolShapeCNSymbolShape
33triangle8Eoctagon
4Ssquare12Bcuboctahedron
4Ttetrahedron12Iicosahedron
5Qsquare pyramid12Utruncated tetrahedron
6Ooctahedron12Xhexagonal prism
6Ptrigonal prism12Ddodecagon
6Hhexagon16Goctagonal prism
7Vhexagonal pyramid24Ktruncated octahedron
8Ccube24Rrhombicuboctahedron
8Asquare antiprism24M / Wdodecagonal prism / truncated cube

Shapes are measured from node centroids in your structure, so strong distortion (RMS above ~18°) is flagged “strongly distorted”. Rectangles still count as S, and flattened tetrahedra may read as S.

Figures & export

  • Display panel: atom style (faded is best with the net), colour by building unit or element, packing (a, b, c limits from/to, e.g. 0–2 or −0.5–1.5, keeping whole fragments whose atom or centroid lies inside the limits), node size, edge width, H atoms, guests, node labels, vertex figures, the figure background, and Net colours: click a swatch to recolour a node class or the net edges with the hex colour picker (or type #RRGGBB). Colours apply to the structure, ideal net, legend and coordination-sequence plot, and reset when a new file is opened.
  • Figure PNG / SVG saves the view in the active tab (structure, ideal net, a building-unit card, or the coordination-sequence plot on the Invariants tab). Pick 2–4× resolution for print; choose a transparent background for slides.
  • Net (.cgd) saves the simplified net in Systre format for cross-checking in Systre or ToposPro.
  • Invariants CSV and Report (.txt) save the numbers for your records or SI.
  • Drag the divider next to the side panel to resize it; double-click to reset.

Troubleshooting

“No periodic framework found”
Bonds between the building units were not detected. Raise the bond tolerance to 0.5–0.6 Å, or check that the CIF has symmetry operators or a recognised space group.
Wrong or too many SBUs
If a paddle-wheel splits into two metals, raise Max M···M. If two clusters merge into one, lower it.
Porphyrin or macrocycle split into several nodes
Increase Largest ring kept as one unit (e.g. 16–20).
Unexpected extra nodes or odd connectivity
Usually disorder or leftover solvent bonded to the framework. Turn on Guests and H atoms in Display to inspect, and read the notes at the bottom of the Invariants tab.
Rod MOFs (MOF-74, MIL-53)
Infinite metal-oxide rods are split into single-metal nodes, and the app shows a warning. The accepted descriptions of rod MOFs use rod packings or points-of-extension nets, so use ToposPro or CrystalNets.jl for these.
Result depends on settings
Changing any analysis setting re-runs the analysis automatically; Re-analyse repeats it with the current settings.

Limits

  • Nets are named by coordination sequences (10 shells) and point symbols, not by a full graph isomorphism test (Systre key). A few different nets share these invariants and are reported together.
  • The library holds 2,400+ RCSR nets with coordinates plus the 2D nets hcb, sql, kgm, hxl, kgd and fes. Newer nets, some RC 3.2 derived nets and non-crystallographic nets can only be named tentatively or not at all.
  • Node classes are grouped by coordination sequence, so the transitivity shown is a lower bound on the true number of symmetry-distinct nodes and edges.
  • Heavily disordered structures may need a cleaned CIF (one disorder component, no partial solvent).

Glossary

SBU
Secondary building unit: a metal cluster with its bridging atoms.
Point of extension
The atom where a linker attaches to an SBU (e.g. a carboxylate carbon); it fixes the SBU’s connectivity and shape.
Coordination sequence (CS)
The number of nodes 1, 2, 3 … bonds away from a node. TD10 is 1 plus the sum of the first ten terms.
Point symbol
The shortest circuit through each pair of edges at a node.
Transitivity [p q]
The number of kinds of node (p) and edge (q). Edge-transitive nets have q = 1; minimal-transitivity trinodal nets have [3 2].
Interpenetration
Several identical nets occupying the same crystal without sharing bonds.
Augmented net (-a)
A net with each vertex replaced by its vertex figure, showing the shape a building unit must have.

References

  • RCSR, the Reticular Chemistry Structure Resource: M. O’Keeffe, M. A. Peskov, S. J. Ramsden, O. M. Yaghi, Acc. Chem. Res. 2008, 41, 1782 (rcsr.net). Net data from the RCSR set bundled with PORMAKE (MIT licence).
  • Z. Chen, H. Jiang, M. Li, M. O’Keeffe, M. Eddaoudi, “Reticular Chemistry 3.2”, Chem. Rev. 2020, 120, 8039.
  • F. Hoffmann, MOF nets list, The Fascination of Crystals and Symmetry (crystalsymmetry.wordpress.com).
  • Cross-checking tools: Systre (gavrog.org), ToposPro (topospro.com), CrystalNets.jl.
